newsitem.title: USA: Gore's political influence on Clinton rises.
newsitem.headline: Gore's political influence on Clinton rises.

text.p: With the abrupt departure of guru Dick Morris, Vice President Al Gore is increasingly emerging as President Bill Clinton's chief political adviser and advocate for the "sensible center" in policy debates.

Gore, already one of the most influential vice presidents in U.S. history because of his unusually close chemistry with Clinton, has been filling the vacuum created by the loss of Morris -- a political adviser credited with turning Clinton's bleak political fortunes after the 1994 Republican congressional elections landslide.

According to campaign insiders, there has been a subtle change in Gore's role since late August, when Morris was forced to resign hours after a prostitute said he had been sharing secrets and a bed with her.

Until then, Morris had been the person pushing Clinton to the centre of the political spectrum -- frequently clashing with the liberal advocates in the White House, like presidential adviser George Stephanopoulos and Harold Ickes, a deputy chief of staff.

Gore, a participant at virtually all of the weekly evening political strategy sessions held at the White House for more than a year and a half, had acted more as a mediator than an advocate -- trying to bring the warring factions together.

"The vice president before was often times the middleman between Morris on the one side and whoever on the other -- George or Harold," one senior administration official said. "He would not take sides there."
"Dick was always the person who advocated for the centre and I think now the vice president is fulfilling more of that role, just because that's where he is anyway," the official said.
"Now with Dick gone, the vice president is helping the president stay kind of in the sensible centre," the official said.

Although some White House and campaign officials sought to downplay the ideological debate within the Clinton camp, none disagreed with the view that Gore has extensive influence and that it has been growing.

"It is fair to say that the president has always relied very closely on Al Gore for advice," said White House Political Director Doug Sosnik. "And I think, as he gets to the final days of the campaign, he's relying on the vice president even more."

A senior administration official, discussing the impact of Morris' removal, said that "while it was true before, it is even more true now that the president bounces more ideas off Al Gore than anyone else ... He's probably more active now in terms of brainstorming, vetting ideas and things like that."

White House Press Secretary Mike McCurry said Morris "did play the role of political strategist and, with him gone, frankly a lot of people have emerged now in their areas of expertise." He singled out Sosnick, independent pollster Mark Penn and White House Chief of Staff Leon Panetta.
"Everyone has been elevated in their role, but the one who has taken on the role of the most important personal confidant of the president is the vice president," McCurry said.

The close relationship between Clinton and Gore can be traced to several bonds, including the fact they are close in age -- Clinton has just turned 50 and Gore is 48. Both also admit to being "policy wonks."
A recent Rose Garden ceremony offers insights into their relationship. A reporter asked Clinton a question -- prompting a fairly lengthy response.
Then came a tap on Clinton's shoulder. "Could I say something?" Gore interrupted. He then made some points as Clinton stood by smiling and nodding in agreement.
In the past, no vice president would have dared to do that, certainly not Dan Quayle to President George Bush, nor would Bush have considered doing it as Ronald Reagan's vice president.
In fact, the most remarkable part of the incident was that it was not considered remarkable.
